title: HTTP / HTTPS
objectives: Read an HTTP request/response and its status codes
Describe what HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 improve

sections.markdown: HTTP is a stateless request/response protocol at the application layer. HTTPS is HTTP carried inside a TLS-encrypted channel.

sections.code:
GET /api/products?id=42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGci...
Accept: application/json

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{ "id": 42, "name": "GS1 Widget" }

sections.markdown: **Safe** = no server state change. **Idempotent** = N calls == 1 call. Is POST idempotent? No. Is DELETE? Yes — deleting twice leaves it deleted.

## HTTP versions
- **HTTP/1.1**: persistent connections, one request at a time per connection.
- **HTTP/2**: multiplexed streams + header compression — no app-layer head-of-line blocking.
- **HTTP/3**: runs over QUIC (UDP) to remove TCP head-of-line blocking.
Putting auth tokens or secrets in the URL query string — URLs leak into logs, history and Referer headers. Use headers or the body.

flashcards.back: Safe = no state change (GET). Idempotent = N calls equal 1 call (GET, PUT, DELETE — not POST).
401 = not authenticated (who are you?). 403 = authenticated but not allowed (you can't do this).
It lets many requests share one connection without waiting in line (app-layer head-of-line blocking).

quiz.explain: POST typically creates a new resource each time, so repeating it has additional effects.
401 Unauthorized means authentication is required/failed; 403 is authenticated-but-forbidden.
HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP to avoid TCP head-of-line blocking and speed up handshakes.
5xx are server errors; 503 means the server is temporarily unavailable.
